title: Deeds as soil, the Word as seed
hook: make good deeds the soil and the Word the seed, and water it with truth (Sri Rag, ang 24)

segments.voice: Yesterday, sach, truth. Your line was truth, lived. Did you say the small truth you'd usually skip? Today, Guru Nanak takes that same idea out to a farm. Day two hundred fifty.

Ask any farmer in the Punjab, or anyone who's kept a tomato plant alive on a balcony: the seed is the easy part. A packet costs almost nothing. What decides the harvest is the ground you put it in, and whether you water it, day after day, when nothing seems to be happening. Tradition remembers Guru Nanak as a farmer in his last years, and his hymns are full of fields, plows and rain. On day 145 we heard one of them, the mind as plowman. Today, a different one, a whole spiritual life in a single line. Deeds as soil.
screen: `THE SEED IS THE EASY PART.` → `THE GROUND DECIDES.` → `NANAK THE FARMER.`

segments.voice: On Ang 24, in Sri Rag, Guru Nanak sings: amal kar dhartee beej sabdo kar sach kee aab nit dehi paanee. Make your deeds the earth, make the Word the seed, and water it every day with the water of truth. Then, in paraphrase: become that kind of farmer, and faith will sprout. Look at the three parts. Amal, deeds, is the soil. Sabad, the Guru's Word, is the seed. Sach, yesterday's word, is the water, and nit means every day. Each needs the others. A beautiful seed in hard, stony ground won't grow: that's someone who hears wonderful hymns and changes nothing in how they act. Good soil with no seed is honest work with no remembering. And soil and seed with no water is a promising start that dries out by Thursday. The picture also says something quietly about time. Farmers don't dig up a seed every morning to see if it's working. They water and wait. The next line says that whoever farms this way comes to understand heaven and hell, and many readers hear in it that both grow from how you live. And it fits the man who sang it. Tradition tells that after decades of travel, Guru Nanak settled at Kartarpur on the Ravi River and worked the land himself, with a community that farmed, sang and ate together. The teacher of the Word was also a man with dirt under his nails.
screen: `AMAL — DEEDS ARE THE SOIL.` · `SABAD — THE WORD IS THE SEED.` · `SACH — TRUTH IS THE WATER.` · `WATER AND WAIT.` · then, large: `DEEDS ARE THE SOIL.`

segments.voice: Picture a small patch of ground. That's today. Now choose one good deed to plant in it: a meal cooked for someone, a bill paid on time, an hour of help, a kind word to someone who won't expect it. Picture putting it in the ground. You don't need to see it grow. Just plant it, and resolve to water it. Then rest with the breath, patient as a farmer. The bell holds the time.
Amal, deeds, the soil of the spiritual life. Guru Nanak's farming picture in Sri Rag: good deeds are the ground, the Word is the seed, and truth, given every day, is the water.
Your line: deeds are the soil. Today, plant the one good deed you chose, and don't dig it up to check. Day two hundred fifty.

screen: `DAY 250 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: RISING SPIRITS, GOOD FOR ALL.`

howItsDone: Sikhs often cite Guru Nanak's years farming at Kartarpur as the model of a householder's life, joining honest work, remembering the Name and sharing, and his farming images are sung in kirtan.

myth: in this hymn, the Word is the soil and deeds are the seed
deeds are the soil, the Word is the seed, and truth is the water.

nit dehi paanee: water it daily with truth.

fork.setup: you've heard beautiful hymns for years, but nothing in how you act has changed. in Guru Nanak's picture, what's missing?
options: the soil: good deeds for the Word to grow in.
fork.reveal: a fine seed in stony ground won't grow. amal kar dhartee: make your deeds the earth.

original.note: Gurmukhi: amal, deeds; a word from Persian and Arabic that Guru Nanak uses for the soil of the spiritual life.

trapdoor: what you thought: good deeds and faith are two separate things.
what it means: deeds are the ground the Word grows in, and truth, given daily, is the water; each needs the others.
what a scholar hears: Sri Rag Mahala 1, Ang 24; amal (Perso-Arabic, 'deeds'), sabad (the Word) and aab (Persian, 'water') mix languages, as Guru Nanak often did for mixed audiences.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 24 (Sri Rag Mahala 1)

notes: Word is the title's head per the outline.

Transliteration of the Ang 24 line should be confirmed; the next line (hoe kirsaan eemaan jammaae lai bhisat dojak moorre ev jaanee) is paraphrased as 'become that kind of farmer, and faith will sprout... learn what heaven and hell really are'. Confirm the reading.
Amal and aab identified as Perso-Arabic/Persian loanwords; confirm.
Kartarpur on the Ravi and Guru Nanak's farming life are from tradition; stated as such.

Audit (second sample): the hook's 'Guru Nanak spent his last years farming at Kartarpur' was a near-copy of day 145's hook and stated tradition as fact; it now says tradition remembers him as a farmer and points back to day 145's farming hymn (Ang 595). The teach no longer presents 'heaven and hell are not places you're sent' as the hymn's own claim; it is now a reading many hold.
